notes: Schedule 1 Children Act case management; Singer J strikes out further housing settlement and limits lump sum claims.

enrichment.short_title: JP v JRP: second Schedule 1 property adjustment and lump sum claims struck out
key_facts: An unmarried mother applied under Schedule 1 of the Children Act 1989 for further financial provision for her 10-year-old daughter, including a larger home, refurbishment, a car and secured school fees.
In 1996 Johnson J had ordered the father to settle a £90,000 home and pay a lump sum; the father complied and the child lived in the settled flat.
The mother sought about £700,000 to upgrade housing partly to accommodate a younger half-sibling for whom the father owed no duty.
Parallel Child Support Agency proceedings remained unresolved and the father was paying school fees and about £450 per month maintenance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court case management hearing on whether further Schedule 1 settlement, transfer and lump sum claims should proceed to trial.
enrichment.outcome: The application for a further settlement of property was struck out; the transfer of property application was dismissed; the attempt to fund upgraded housing by lump sum was ruled legally impossible; limited lump sum and school-fee issues were case-managed to trial with the mother ordered to pay the father's costs of the hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Under Schedule 1 paragraph 1(5)(b) a parent may receive only one property adjustment order—settlement or transfer—against the same person for the same child, so a further settlement precludes a transfer application; lump sums cannot be used to circumvent that prohibition or to replicate a reversionary housing settlement.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 1(5)(b) bars a transfer order after an earlier settlement order
Whether a second lump sum may fund upgraded accommodation subject to reversion
Jurisdiction to make periodical payments where the Child Support Act applies
Whether the mother's capital claims were proportionate case management for trial

notes: Landmark immigration detention appeal; Brooke LJ allows Roma family's false imprisonment claim to proceed.

enrichment.short_title: ID v Home Office: immigration detention, false imprisonment and officer immunity
key_facts: A Czech Roma family claimed asylum on arrival; the father was detained overnight while the mother and daughters were initially given temporary admission.
The family was later detained at Oakington and Yarl's Wood after asylum was refused; they alleged unlawful detention, discrimination and Convention breaches.
District Judge Lightman struck out the Home Office's strike-out application; Judge Crawford Lindsay QC reversed that on appeal.
The claimants sought declarations under the Human Rights Act, race and sex discrimination findings, and damages for false imprisonment and negligence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from county court orders granting the Home Office summary disposal of most claims in an immigration detention action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the matter remitted to the county court for case management and trial of false imprisonment and related claims; immigration officers were held not entitled to broad immunity comparable to courts.
enrichment.ratio: Persons subject to Schedule 2 immigration detention retain protected liberty interests under Article 5 and the common law; if detention is unlawful, immigration officers are not generally immune from false imprisonment claims merely because they acted without bad faith, and published proportionate policies must govern administrative detention.
legal_issues: Whether Schedule 2 detainees are in a special category with weaker liberty protection
Immunity of immigration officers from false imprisonment after Anisminic
Interaction of false imprisonment, Article 5 ECHR and administrative detention
Whether strike-out or summary judgment was appropriate on the pleaded claims

notes: Repeated infant shaking case; eight-year total sentence upheld on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: R v RD: consecutive sentences for repeated shaking and punching of baby
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to assault occasioning ABH and causing GBH with intent to his two-to-three-month-old son after the mother left him alone with the children.
On 17 March 2004 he squeezed the baby hard enough to fracture 14 ribs and shook him; on 2 April he shook the baby for about two minutes, punched his head repeatedly and dropped him on the floor.
The child suffered skull fracture, subdural haemorrhage and later profound disability with microcephaly and infantile spasms.
He was sentenced to six years on the section 18 count and two years consecutive on the ABH count, totalling eight years after a guilty plea.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge on totality and length grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the total eight-year sentence on plea was held appropriate for two sustained non-accidental assaults that nearly caused death.
enrichment.ratio: Repeated life-threatening violence against a very young child may justify consecutive sentences where there were two distinct incidents; manslaughter sentencing ranges are of limited assistance where section 18 specific intent is admitted and the injuries were nearly fatal.
legal_issues: Whether consecutive sentences breached the totality principle
Appropriate starting point for section 18 baby-shaking offences on plea
Relevance of manslaughter sentencing authorities
Weight to be given to mitigation, remorse and psychiatric reports

notes: House of Lords constitution on delayed employment tribunal decisions and Article 6 appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Bangs v Connex: Article 6 and appeals from delayed employment tribunal decisions
key_facts: Mr Bangs, a black African ticket examiner, alleged direct race discrimination after Connex investigated chargebacks, dismissed him and later demoted him following an internal appeal.
The employment tribunal heard eight days of evidence in 2002 but did not promulgate its decision until August 2003, over a year later.
The employment appeal tribunal set aside the race discrimination finding as unsafe because of delay-related errors and omissions.
Connex cross-appealed contending the tribunal findings were perverse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the House of Lords on whether unreasonable tribunal delay gives an independent ground of appeal beyond questions of law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; the employment tribunal decision stood and the case proceeded to remedies; delay alone did not show loss of a fair trial.
enrichment.ratio: Section 21 limits employment tribunal appeals to questions of law; unreasonable delay is not an independent ground of appeal merely because a decision is factually unsafe, but exceptional delay may raise a question of law if it creates a real risk of denial of a fair trial under Article 6.
legal_issues: Whether Cobham v Frett unsafe-decision test applies to employment tribunal appeals
Construction of section 21(1) after the Human Rights Act 1998
Whether delayed credibility findings were perverse or procedurally unfair
Appropriate remedy where tribunal delay exceeded reasonable targets

Porter v Magill [2002] 2 AC 357
Yeboah v Crofton [2002] IRLR 634

notes: Liquidator discontinue misfeasance claim; Court of Appeal restores normal CPR 38.6 costs order.

enrichment.short_title: Walker v Walker: liquidator's late discontinuance and costs under CPR 38.6
key_facts: The liquidator of Walker Windsail Systems Plc pursued misfeasance and fraudulent trading claims of about £500,000 against Mr and Mrs Walker under freezing injunctions granted in 1999.
Disclosed assets were about £292,000; proceedings were conjoined with disqualification proceedings and Mrs Walker died in 2001.
After years of litigation funded from released frozen assets and a life policy, the liquidator sought leave to discontinue because further prosecution was commercially worthless.
The judge permitted discontinuance with no order as to costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against permission to discontinue misfeasance proceedings without an order that the liquidator pay the defendants' costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the no-costs order was set aside and the liquidator ordered to pay the defendants' costs to the date of discontinuance; interim payment of £25,000 ordered subject to receipts.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 38.6 the normal rule on discontinuance is that the claimant pays the defendant's costs unless there is good reason to depart; a liquidator cannot walk away without costs where the commercial futility of the claim was apparent from the outset and relevant factors had not materially changed.
legal_issues: Application of CPR 38.6 to a liquidator discontinuing misfeasance proceedings
Whether changed asset position justified no order as to costs
Relevance of Stratford v Lindley and post-CPR discontinuance authorities
Exercise of discretion where freezing orders funded defence costs

notes: Habeas corpus extradition challenge to France dismissed; in absentia conviction challenge rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Re Hewitson: habeas corpus challenge to French cannabis extradition
key_facts: French customs seized 89.2 kilograms of cannabis resin from two brothers who implicated the applicant as organiser of the trafficking.
The applicant was arrested under a provisional warrant and the Secretary of State gave authority to proceed with extradition to France.
A letter unlawfully seized from the applicant's premises had featured in a French confrontation interview, but the Divisional Court had earlier ordered its return.
France later convicted the applicant in absentia to nine years' imprisonment while extradition proceedings continued in England.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application challenging lawfulness of committal for extradition to France.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the Secretary of State had sufficient information to authorise proceedings without relying on unlawfully obtained material, and the applicant could set aside the in absentia conviction on return to France.
enrichment.ratio: Even assuming unlawfully obtained material was considered, ample independent information justified authority to proceed under section 7(2); where an accused person may set aside an in absentia conviction on return, section 6 does not prevent extradition and section 11(3)(c) does not make return oppressive.
legal_issues: Effect of unlawfully seized evidence on section 7 authority to proceed
Whether in absentia conviction rendered return unjust under section 6
Application of Krombach v France and Foy v Governor of Brixton
Whether accusation case or conviction case governed the extradition request

notes: Formula One sponsorship conditional payment-in order reduced on appeal; shares escrow permitted.

enrichment.short_title: Jordan Grand Prix v Tiger Telematics: conditional order and misrepresentation defence
key_facts: Jordan Grand Prix sued Tiger Telematics for unpaid Formula 1 sponsorship fees of about US $750,000 under 2003 and 2004 agreements.
Tiger alleged pre-contract misrepresentations about Vodafone litigation, Mercedes engines, drivers and team prospects after a damaging judgment against Jordan.
Master Eyre refused summary judgment but ordered payment into court of US $2.5 million in default of which judgment would be entered.
Tiger argued the defence was shadowy and that Clause 17 termination provisions and its launch finance constraints were ignored.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conditional order under CPR Part 24 requiring payment into court where defence of misrepresentation was possible but improbable.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal the making of the conditional order refused; the amount was reduced to US $1.5 million payable by shares in escrow until shortly before trial, with cash alternative before trial.
enrichment.ratio: A court may dismiss summary judgment yet make a conditional order where a defence may succeed but is improbable; quantum must reflect arguable contractual termination points and the defendant's financial constraints, and need not always require immediate cash payment.
legal_issues: Test for conditional orders under CPR 24 PD.4
Whether alleged sponsorship misrepresentations had a real prospect of success
Construction of termination and repudiation under Clause 17
Appropriate payment-in amount and form where launch funding was sensitive

notes: Extradition habeas corpus claim dismissed for failure to appear; adjournment refused.

enrichment.short_title: Demiray v Holloway: habeas corpus dismissed for non-appearance
key_facts: A Turkish Cypriot applicant challenged detention pending extradition to Turkey on forgery and theft charges.
He had been committed on conditional bail in May 2004 awaiting the Secretary of State's extradition decision.
The claim form alleged delay by the Turkish authorities but no supporting statement was filed; only brief medical notes were sent.
When the case was called on, neither the applicant nor any representative appeared.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for adjournment and writ of habeas corpus in extradition detention proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment refused and the claim dismissed because the applicant failed to appear or ensure representation to pursue it.
enrichment.ratio: Where a habeas corpus claimant does not appear and provides no adequate medical or other basis for adjournment, the court may dismiss the claim rather than adjourn indefinitely.
legal_issues: Whether medical certificates justified adjourning habeas corpus proceedings
Effect of non-appearance on an extradition habeas corpus claim
Whether delay in the extradition process was properly pleaded

notes: Coal mining subsidence arbitration; permission to appeal refused on Section 19 and Section 12 questions.

enrichment.short_title: Coal Authority v Nostell Trust: listed building subsidence repairs under section 19
key_facts: Subsidence damaged the Grade I listed Stable Block at Nostell Priory; the Coal Authority was liable for remedial works.
An arbitrator awarded about £191,000 for future repairs and £12,500 for emergency interior works already carried out.
The Authority challenged the scope of section 19 listed-building repairs and section 12 emergency works procedures.
The arbitrator preferred detailed rebuilding and stone replacement over cosmetic repairs proposed by the Authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996 for permission to appeal an arbitrator's award on questions of law.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on all nine questions; section 19 issues were of public importance but not open to serious doubt, and section 12 issues did not substantially affect the parties' rights.
enrichment.ratio: Section 19 requires remedial works that restore a listed building to its former condition so as to maintain its character of special interest; that does not automatically require premium durability beyond pre-damage condition, but detailed repairs may be chosen where cosmetic works would not maintain special interest.
legal_issues: Whether section 19(1) required a finding that special interest character was affected
Whether section 19(2) mandated especially thorough or durable repairs for listed buildings
Compliance with section 12 notice and inspection requirements for emergency works
Section 69 criteria for permission to appeal arbitration awards

notes: Major VAT carousel fraud confiscation appeal; joint benefit and legitimate expectation issues resolved.

enrichment.short_title: R v May: VAT carousel fraud confiscation and joint control benefit
key_facts: Five defendants pleaded guilty or were convicted of conspiracy to cheat the public revenue through missing-trader VAT carousel fraud costing about £12 million.
Four importing companies sequentially retained VAT on EU computer component sales while goods were re-exported through buffer companies.
Confiscation orders totalled millions of pounds; the judge treated joint controllers as benefiting in the full VAT retained by their companies.
Stapleton and Bravard relied on a pre-plea judicial indication that only provable assets would be considered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against confiscation orders under the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and sentence appeals by May and Lawrence.
enrichment.outcome: Confiscation appeals partly allowed: Stapleton and Bravard orders reduced to identifiable assets for legitimate expectation; Fowles reduced to £40,000 wages; May's confiscation dismissed but sentence reduced from five to four years; Lawrence's sentence appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where conspirators jointly control corporate vehicles used in fraud, each may be treated as obtaining the whole VAT benefit for confiscation purposes; a judge's pre-plea indication that only provable assets will be considered can create a legitimate expectation limiting hidden-asset findings, and a sentencing judge is bound by an agreed basis of plea in confiscation proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether joint controllers each benefit in the full company VAT loss without apportionment
Immunity of ex parte PII material in judge-led confiscation proceedings
Legitimate expectation from pre-plea indications about provable assets
Binding effect of agreed basis of plea on benefit assessment

R v Simpson [1998] 2 Cr App R(S) 111
